# Brief: Amira (PERSONA-013)
## Upcoming Meeting: 2026-05-05

## Since Last Meeting

The budget passed on April 7, and the percussion ed tech position at Memorial was cut. Your friend group already knows — 32 people sent emails and several spoke at the meeting trying to save it, just like last year. This time, the administration had a slide ready to argue back, and it didn't work. Then on April 13, the board got around $300,000 from the teachers' union's trip to Augusta and voted 3–2 to put it into reserves instead of bringing anyone back. Two PE teachers, computer science, and a STEM teacher at Memorial are also listed in the cuts. No new developments since then.

## Open Questions

- Are there really going to be no percussion at all next year, or will someone else cover bits and pieces of it?
- If band goes to half-time later, when would we find out — before the school year ends, or would we just show up in September and it's half what it was?
- Two PE teachers gone means bigger gym classes — how do you even run gym with 40 kids in the room?
- The computer science and STEM teachers were cut — does that mean those classes just disappear from next year's schedule?
- If $300,000 came from Augusta and the board chose reserves over people, what would actually make them choose people next time?
- Nobody asked students what we thought about any of this — is there a way for that to change before next year starts?
- My parents keep hearing about property taxes going up because of Mahoney — if taxpayers are already stressed, does that mean next year's school budget gets even smaller?

## Agenda Implications

No agenda is available for the May 5 meeting yet. Based on where things stand, here's what to prepare for:

**What might come up:** The budget has already passed the board, so major decisions about who gets cut are probably settled unless something unexpected changes. The meeting may cover implementation details — how the cuts actually get scheduled, which programs shrink, what next year actually looks like. This is the part that directly shapes your daily life even though it doesn't sound like a "big vote."

**What this means for you:** The decisions about *how* cuts are applied — not just *which* cuts — will determine whether band can keep going in some form or not, whether STEM and computer science become electives only, and whether your class sizes feel different in September.

**What to listen for:** Any mention of Memorial specifically. Any discussion of how the percussion position's duties get redistributed. Any talk about enrichment or gifted-and-talented programming — cuts compound, and programs that feel stable one year can shift silently the next.

**What to prepare:** If there's a public comment period and you or your parents want to speak, the most effective thing at this stage isn't re-arguing the already-decided cuts — it's asking what the plan is for students in the programs that are shrinking. "I'm a 7th grader in band at Memorial. What does band look like for me next year?" That's a concrete question an administrator can answer on the record.

## Watch For

- Any mention of "staffing allocations by building" — that's where you'd hear whether Memorial specifically gets hit again or whether cuts are spread differently next time
- Superintendent or board members using the phrase "enrichment" — pay attention, because that's the category band, STEM, and computer science fall into, and more cuts there affect your school day directly
- Councilor Scott, who was the first elected official to connect immigration enforcement to lost students — if he speaks, he's the one who has framed problems in terms of what kids actually experience
- Any reference to "student voice" or "student advisory" — this could be a real opening for getting students asked before decisions happen, or it could be just words. Listen for whether someone proposes an actual mechanism (a student rep on a committee, a survey before cuts, etc.)
- Watch for whether the board talks about reserves again — if they mention the $300,000 in reserves, ask yourself: what conditions would make them spend it on people instead of holding it? If they name those conditions, you'll know what the threshold is for next time
- Your mother might be interested in any discussion of property tax rates and school funding together, since she's worried about both — if a board member or councilor makes that connection, it could help answer the "why can we afford a turf field but not band" question you've been stuck on
- If anyone asks about the 2026–27 school year planning timeline, listen — that's your signal for when the next round of decisions starts, and getting student input into that process early matters more than weighing in at the end
